title: Engage in a range of speaking/signing and listening interactions for a variety of purposes

lessons.title: Listening well at work
lessons.html:
Why listening matters

In a stable yard many instructions are spoken, not written. "Give Duke only half a scoop tonight." "Do not turn out the grey mare, she is lame." If you do not listen well, a horse can get hurt. Good listening keeps horses and people safe.

How to listen well

  1. Stop and look. Stop what you are doing. Look at the person speaking.
  2. Pay attention. Do not think about something else. Put your phone away.
  3. Listen for the main point. What must I do? To which horse? When?
  4. Ask if you do not understand. "Do you mean the bay horse in stable 6?"
  5. Repeat it back. "So, half a scoop for Duke tonight. Okay."

Repeating back is very important. It shows the speaker you understood. If you got it wrong, they can correct you at once.

Things that block listening

  • Noise: a tractor, a radio, horses calling
  • Being in a hurry
  • Thinking you already know what the person will say
  • Not liking the speaker
  • Different home languages

If it is noisy, move to a quieter place. If you speak a different language from the speaker, use simple words, show with your hands, or ask a co-worker to help.

Body language

We also talk with our bodies. Nodding shows you understand. Crossed arms and looking away can show you are not interested. A friendly face makes people want to talk to you.

Horses also use body language: ears pinned back means angry; ears forward means interested. Good grooms listen to horses with their eyes.

Example

The vet tells Nomsa: "Cold hose his leg for 15 minutes, twice a day." Nomsa repeats: "Fifteen minutes, morning and afternoon, right front leg?" The vet says: "Left front." Nomsa's question stopped a mistake.

lessons.title: Speaking clearly for different purposes
lessons.html:
We speak for many reasons

PurposeExample
To give information"The farrier is coming at 10:00."
To report a problem"Storm has a swollen hind leg."
To ask for something"Can I have new gloves, please?"
To give instructions"Lead the horse on the left side."
To be friendly"Good morning, how was your weekend?"

Speaking clearly

  • Think before you speak: what do I want to say?
  • Speak loud enough and not too fast.
  • Use simple words the listener knows.
  • Say the most important thing first.
  • Look at the person.

Reporting a problem

When you report a problem to your supervisor, say:

  1. Who - which horse or person
  2. What - what you saw
  3. Where - which stable or camp
  4. When - when you noticed

Example: "Storm, in stable 3, is not eating and keeps lying down and rolling. I saw it at 7 o'clock." This tells the supervisor everything needed to call the vet quickly. Colic is an emergency, so report at once.

Using the phone or radio

Say your name first. Speak slowly. Give the message. Ask the other person to repeat important details. In an emergency, say where you are first.

Being polite

Use please and thank you. Do not shout at co-workers or at horses. If you disagree, speak calmly and explain why. Respect people of different languages and cultures. Wait for your turn to speak in a meeting.

Signing

Some co-workers may be Deaf and use South African Sign Language. Face them, get their attention with a gentle wave or touch on the shoulder, and do not cover your mouth. Learn a few basic signs; it shows respect.

Key points

  • Stop, look, listen and repeat instructions back.
  • Ask questions when you are not sure.
  • Speak clearly, simply and say the most important thing first.
  • Report problems with who, what, where and when.
  • Be polite and respect different languages, including sign language.

quiz.question: Why should you repeat an instruction back to the speaker?

options.text: To show you understood and let them correct mistakes

quiz.question: What should you do first when someone gives you an instruction?
